utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Good morning. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning to the technical booth. Good morning, interpreters. Good morning, legal assistants and court reporters. Good morning, Ms. Hollis, Mr. Saxon. Good morning, Defence counsel. I think they are all present. We are resuming our hearings, and we apologise for the slight delay. We planned to begin at 9.00 because the Chamber has to conclude the hearing at 2.00. We wanted to work for the same amount of hours, and that is why we started early. In any event, we will finish at 2.00, and we are going to have two 20-minute breaks in order to manage the time properly. As you know, tomorrow we are going to have a Status Conference at 4.00 to convey to you the rulings of the Chamber regarding a number of outstanding issues, and we are also going to hear the arguments of the Zigic Defence in respect to the defence of alibi. We are ready now to begin and to resume the hearings. I turn to Ms. Hollis. You have the floor, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning. Your Honour, the Prosecution calls Zlata Cikota.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ms. Zlata Cikota. Can you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are going to read the solemn declaration that the usher is holding out to you, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you comfortable, madam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. But if I may say something. I promised myself in the concentration camp, I took an oath, that if I survived the camp, the concentration camp in Omarska, that I would write a book, and the name of the book is, "I Remember and I Testify."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You are now going to testify, madam, and in order to do so, you will be answering questions which Ms. Hollis is going to put to you. Ms. Hollis, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Would you please state for the record your name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: My maiden name is Medic; married name Cikota. What was the other question?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is your first name, and what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I was born in Gornja Sanica on the 6th of May, 1941.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your first name is Zlata; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You said that you were born in Gornja Sanica. Where is that located?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: It is Western Bosnia, Kljuc municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you move from Kljuc to Tuzla and attend high school in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time if the Prosecution could offer what has previously been marked 2/1.1 [Realtime transcript read in error "2/3.1"] and ask that it be provided to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for interrupting you, Ms. Hollis, but the exhibit has been marked 2/1.1?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just in order to correct the transcript. Thank you. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If I could ask the witness to please take a moment to orient herself to the exhibit. If you could please take the pointer, and for the Judges, point out to them where opstina Kljuc is located.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Opstina Kljuc is this area here. And Gornja Sanica is about 16 kilometres away from Kljuc, in the direction of Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you could also point to opstina Tuzla for the Judges, please.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Tuzla is here. That's where I went to secondary technical school.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you graduate from university in Slovenia with a degree in engineering?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Not mechanical engineering but metal engineering. I'm a graduate engineer of metallurgy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid I can't hear the interpretation at all. Something is wrong with the headphones. I can hear now.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I am a graduate engineer of metallurgy rather than mechanical engineering.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Perhaps there is a problem with the interpretation because I did not say mechanical engineering. I'll try to speak more clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: From 1973 until 1977, did you work as a metallurgic engineer with the steel company that owned the Omarska mining site?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I'm afraid they didn't interpret that right. In that period I did work, but in the iron ore mines at Ljubija, not the steelworks, because the iron ore mine doesn't have a steelworks. There are the steelworks in Josanica, in Sisak, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us what work, if any, you did regarding the Omarska mining site?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I worked on the preparation and construction of the ironworks which had been planned to be constructed in Omarska. And since it proved to be economically infeasible, we worked on the mine itself, that is, the Omarska mines.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: From 1978 until 1985, did you work for the EKK ceramic factory?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you the chief engineer for the Keraterm ceramic plant?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you work at the Prijedor offices of the Privredna Banka Sarajevo from 1985 until May 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were your duties at the Privredna Banka Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I was in the department for review and approval of investment programmes in the whole municipality of Prijedor so I had to review investments.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you present at the founding of the SDS and SDA parties in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall who gave the opening speech for the SDA Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Velida Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was her occupation at that time, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: She was a teacher in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was her ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: She was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mrs. Cikota, what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: That's a difficult question for me to answer. I thought I was a woman of the world, of the free world. In my birth certificate and in my marriage certificate, it says that I am a Yugoslav, and I can prove this. But when I arrived in the Omarska concentration camp, I realised I was a Bosniak and a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you serve as a chairperson of a referendum election committee?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the issue to be decided by that referendum?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: "Are you in favour of a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina" was the question. That was the substance of the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In 1992, were you married to Sead Cikota?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: In his birth certificate, it says he's a Montenegrin. He was in Omarska, like me, and then I realised that he was a Bosniak, a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In 1992, what was his occupation?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: He was secretary for the self-interest community for social insurance, actually for health, what the Germans would call a kranken kasse. It means that the funds for financing hospitals, pharmacies, treatment were managed by him. That is the substance of his job.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was that an important position in the Prijedor community?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Not in the economy, but in the social sector, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In 1992, did you have two sons?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were their ages at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: The younger one, Zlatan, was 12 years old, and the older one, Sejo, was 16.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What property did you have in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I had a three-room apartment at Pecani; I had a garage in my possession which I had purchased; I had a weekend home with land and an orchard around it. And my husband had a family home and a car.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How would you describe your financial situation in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: A normal financial situation for a normal person who worked and lived off his labour. A very normal sort of situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now I'd like to draw your attention to the 23rd of June of 1992. On that date were you taken to the SUP for an informative talk?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were you told about how long you would be gone from your home?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I told I was going for an informative interview, just for this informative talk.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was your husband at home with you on that date?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No. On the 31st of May, he had already been taken away.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know where he had been taken to?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I didn't, but I managed to get in touch with the wife of Drago Prcac so I knew with more or less certainty that he was in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you were taken away on the 23rd of June, were you able to make long-term arrangements for your children?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No, none at all because there was no time. I had to leave the house immediately, in the way I was dressed. There was no time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you arrived at the SUP, what other persons, if any, did you recognise being detained there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: On the right-hand side, in the corridor, there was a bench, and Biba, the dentist was sitting there, Biba Harambasic, her maiden name Pozderac.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was her ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I think she was a Muslim, a Bosniak. Before I didn't care. I didn't even know who was what.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you told why you were brought to the SUP?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you held at the SUP until the 24th of June?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: On that date, were you taken to Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What type of vehicle was used to transport you there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: A black Marica, a police car.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long were you detained at Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Forty-two days. Forty-two days.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you ever told why you were being held there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No. But I was the last woman to be interrogated in Omarska, and then they told me why I was where I was. The investigators who investigated me told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did they tell you as to why you were being held in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: The question they asked was why did I think I was there. Then the next question was what kind of Yugoslavia I was in favour of. The third question was that I had participated in the armed attack on Prijedor and that I was a fundamentalist. Those were the questions that were put me basically.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Had you participated in any kind of attack on anyone?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: For heaven's sake, at my age, with two small children, which woman would do that? Especially a woman like me.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, during the time that you were detained at Omarska, during the nights were you held on the first floor of the restaurant building?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If the witness could please be shown Exhibit 3/77B, Bravo.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And if the witness would please take a moment to familiarise herself with that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If that could be placed on the overhead, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Would you please show the Court what room you were held in at night.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: In B11.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you remember, approximately how many women were held in that room at night?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I think there were 17. I couldn't really tell exactly. There were 35 or 36 of us women in all, so I think there were 17 in this room. I could list them all for you but you would be wasting time. The room was full anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was there a woman who was in charge of that room or had duties regarding that room?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Jadranka Cigelj.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that you recognised Biba Harambasic. Was Biba Harambasic transported with you to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What room was she held in?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: We were together here, behind the door, Biba and myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was there another room on the first floor where other women were held at night?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, in B10. They are next-door rooms, one next to the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And was there a woman who was in charge of that room as well?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you know, who was that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: She was from Kozarac. Zdenka; I think her last name was Rajkovic or Rankovic, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, looking at this diagram, could you tell us, if you know, what the office across from B11 was used for?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I know very well. The room is B5.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was that room used for?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: It was mainly used to accommodate, I don't know how to call them, the commanders, the leaders, the commanders of the concentration camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: During the night while you were held in Omarska, were you ever able to leave your room?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: At night? Frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What would you do when you left your room at night? Why did you leave your room?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: To be quite frank, and I am a frank person, I left most often in order to see Drago Prcac, and sometimes there were two tables here. We called this place a Pejici, and sometimes Jadranka and I would have a smoke here. Right here.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you say "Jadranka," you mean Jadranka Cigelj?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, when you would leave your room in the morning, B11, approximately what time of the morning would you leave that room?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: It wasn't always the same time, but between 5.00 and 6.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who, if any, would tell you to leave your room and go downstairs?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Mostly the shift leaders. They brought us there and took us down again.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: During the day, were you held in the dining room area of the restaurant building?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, that's where we were all day.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: From that dining room area, what areas of the camp were you able to see?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: The pista, the whole of the pista; then this part, the whole of this part; and we could also see from the toilet this part here. So this part here and the whole of this area and the whole of this area. We couldn't see this part here.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the pista, what other buildings were you able to see from the dining room area?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: The "white house" and partly the "red house." Not the whole of it but a part of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that frequently at night you would go out of your room to see Drago Prcac. When you went to see him, what room would he be in?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Drago was always in this room here, B5. In B5.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you went to see him in B5, did you ever see any other camp personnel in that room with him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, very often.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who would you see?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Krkan was always there. When the third shift was on, Krkan would always be there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you if that exhibit could be returned to the registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you have mentioned Prcac, Drago Prcac, and Krkan, and I'll ask you about those in a moment. But before that, I would like to ask you, did you recognise any of the camp personnel at Omarska as people you had known before you were brought to the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, I knew Kvocka from sight. As for the others, I didn't know them because those were not the people I socialised with.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How was it that you knew Kvocka by sight?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I knew him because he used in live in the same area where I lived, at Pecani, a little further down. But we also had family ties because my sister-in-law is his wife's aunt, and his wife's name was Jasminka. I also knew his mother-in-law, Hajra, and his father-in-law, Eso, his wife's father whose name was Eso. I used to go to that house very often, and I also know his brothers-in-law, his wife's brothers, all three of them. Rizo, Ferid, they lived in that area, in Muharem Suljanovic Street, and my brother has a house in the immediate vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you said that Kvocka's wife's father's first name was Eso. What was his last name?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. Crnalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is the ethnicity of the Crnalic family?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: They are Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When was it that you left Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: On the 3rd of August -- yes, on the 3rd of August, in the morning hours of that day, around half past seven, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, during the time period that you were held in Omarska, between the 24th of June and the 3rd of August, during what time period did you see Kvocka in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Kvocka. When I arrived, that is, on the first morning after I had spent my first night there, I saw Kvocka and Slavica Lakic who came from Prijedor in a Mercedes. Slavica Lakic, I know her from 1974 because she used to work as a typist at the Prijedor SUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, this first morning when you saw Kvocka arrive with Slavica Lakic, where were you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I was in the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where did Kvocka arrive in the Mercedes?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Every time he would come with Slavica, he would park his car somewhere near the gate, in that area near the restaurant, that is, somewhere near the last window overlooking the area where meals were served.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would like to offer 3/103 and ask that it be provided to the witness, to the Court, and to the Defence. Your Honours, the reason we have marked this 3/103 is that the Prosecution has marked the statement of Sifeta Susic as 3/102A and B.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mrs. Cikota, if you could take a look at that photograph, and using that photograph, if you could show the Judges where it was that you saw Kvocka and Slavica Lakic that first morning that you were in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: In this area here. He used to park his car here most of the time while he was doing what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: After he parked that car, how did he come into the restaurant that day?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Every time through the window, Slavica and he, they had to pass by this area where we were, and he would enter the area here.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you saw him, in what direction would he be headed after he came in through the window?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Towards us, because we used to sit on the radiators. In this corner here. You can't see it very well, but it was in this area here.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if the witness could be provided 3/77A.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you could take a moment, please, to orient yourself.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I know this. I don't need to orient myself. We were here, in this area. This is where the radiators were, in this part of the room. So he would come in here, through the window, and he would pass by this area and enter through this door, both him and Slavica. I could draw an arrow here. This was the door that he used.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You were originally pointing to an area in room A22 where you said that you would be seated, and that area was --

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: That is the area where meals were served.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: -- and that area was in the corner with the wall of A20; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: This area you pointed to that Kvocka and Slavica Lakic would enter was an area with the number A13. What was that area? What was that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Where is A -- oh, okay. You mean the corridor here, the hall.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. How many times did you see Kvocka come into the camp while you were there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Kvocka did not stay there very long. I don't know how long he stayed but he was replaced. That was the story. That was what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you have any idea today of how long he was in the camp after you arrived?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, in addition to seeing him come to the camp in the morning and come through this dining room area, were there any other areas of the camp that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No, but I did see him once when he came one particular morning, and he called out Braco Burazerovic. This is a man I know very well. I think his name is actually Muhamed but I'm not quite sure. So he called him out and I really did see that he gave him a parcel. Braco approached the Mercedes that Kvocka called him and Braco took the parcel.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you yourself ever have any personal contact with Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened when you had that personal contact?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: One day Kvocka asked who Zlata Cikota was, and I said it was me. I stood up and I approached him, and Kvocka said, "No one should talk to you any more, but I am just informing you that your children are well. Thank you." I even think, but I'm not sure that on that occasion he brought me a small piece of soap and a little towel, so I assume that that had been sent by my brother, but I didn't see him after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you stated that you knew Kvocka's wife's brothers. Did you ever see them in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall how long you had been in the camp when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: If you had been in the camp, you probably wouldn't remember it yourself because it was a matter of life or death, and it is very difficult for myself to orient myself in time. Whether it was at the beginning, or whether it was after ten days, I don't know, but they were there. They had been brought to Omarska and they were accommodated in the "glass house". That "glass house" was a part of the restaurant. And I saw them. I went to them and I asked them how come they were there, and they said that Kvocka had hidden them at his grandparents house, but that was reported by someone. They were discovered and brought to Omarska, and I think that from then on, I didn't see Kvocka any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you have already mentioned Drago Prcac and Krkan. First I'd like to ask you some questions about Drago Prcac. How was it that you came to know Drago Prcac or know of him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Through his son, Ljubisa, who was a very good friend. They went to school together and he used to come to my house very often, so I knew little Ljubisa for a number of years.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: He was a very good friend to whom?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Of my son, my eldest son, Sejo.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When, if ever, did you see Drago Prcac in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Well, I saw him -- I saw him -- I mean, when I arrived in Omarska, on that afternoon when I saw those miserable people lying down on the asphalt surface, when I saw that huge crowd of people, I immediately realised that something was going wrong. So we first came to the restaurant, it was the afternoon so we didn't go to the rooms. The windows were open and I saw a very neat looking man compared to the others, and I called him through the window because I saw that something was happening, and I said, "Excuse me. Could you come here," and he indeed came to us. I didn't know him and I asked him whether he knew Drago Prcac, and he told me he did. I asked him, "Could you please tell him that Zlata Cikota is in the camp, that I am in Omarska." And I was actually surprised by that man. I came to know him later on. After I left the camp I learnt his name, his surname. He did convey the message to Drago, and I think he appeared the next day. Again, through the window I saw a man wearing a white T-shirt, trousers. He was carrying something in his hand. And he wanted to know who Zlata Cikota was, and I said it was me, and he gave me a parcel and I knew exactly what it contained. I was very happy because I realised that he had, indeed, conveyed the message to him. So I felt safer a bit. We didn't have much of a conversation. He simply gave me the parcel, and I went back to that group of women I was with.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, this first time that you saw Drago Prcac in Omarska camp, was Kvocka still in the camp at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No. At least I didn't see him. Well, during the night, we were not allowed to look around. Most of the time we were ordered to keep our heads down. But I managed to see quite a few things thanks to Drago Prcac.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you testified earlier that after a period of days, when you were brought to Omarska, after a period of some days you no longer saw Kvocka in the camp.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: My question is this: This first time you saw Drago Prcac, was this during the time period that Kvocka was still at Omarska, or was this after Kvocka had left Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. Well, no. No. While Kvocka was still there in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, after this first meeting that you had with Drago Prcac, how often did you see him after that in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Whenever his shift was on duty, because I used to follow him. He probably didn't notice me but I observed him because I needed him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You said that you would leave your room often at night to see Drago Prcac. Why did you seek him out?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. Every time I would say, "Drago, please save me or my children, one of us." That was the only thing I managed to say. Just one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Why did you feel Drago Prcac could save you or your family?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Well, I spent 42 days in the Omarska concentration camp and I could observe the situation, and I knew who was who and what kind of influence people had in the camp. And since Drago Prcac, because of Ljubisa, I thought he wouldn't let my children to become orphans. I hoped that he would be humane enough to help me. And I told him, "At least myself or Sead," my husband, but luckily we survived, both of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Why did you believe Drago Prcac was a person of influence in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Well, you can imagine, I spent 42 days in the camp so I was able to realise what was going on and to make some conclusions as to the positions held by various people there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Can you assist --

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I think that Drago, if I may say that, this is my opinion, my assessment -- can I give my opinion here, or do you just want me to answer your questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What I would like you to do is to tell the Judges what you observed or heard that led you to conclude that Drago Prcac was a person of influence in the camp? What was your conclusion based on?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: My conclusions. Well, I think that Drago was the commander in charge of the security of the investigation centre of the Omarska concentration camp. I think that Meakic Zeljko had the same position and I think that Kvocka had the same position and that those three individuals were in charge of the situation in the Omarska concentration camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, could you please try to assist the Judges and tell them why you reached that conclusion. What did you observe, what did you hear to make you conclude that these people held those positions?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: You mean what I based my conclusions on? I don't quite understand your question. Could you please repeat it for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That's exactly what I mean. What did you base your conclusions on? What observations, what other information did you base your conclusions on?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Conclusions. The investigators would also come in the same bus, in the same composition. They were in charge of interrogating those miserable people who were there. They would go to the upper floor, they had contact with them, and this is where the interrogations were held. Very often beatings would also take place. People died there. And all of them, I don't know whether as individuals or in groups, were allowed to come to the concentration camp. I mean, people from the outside, they were allowed to call out anyone they wanted, kill anyone they wanted, beat up people they wanted to beat. The group that was headed by Krle, for example, and the one headed by Ckalja -- let me think, Ckalja, Krle, and Krkan, they were also subordinate to them, and the people who used to come with them in buses, they were so-called shift commanders and they were our torturers. So it means that they had a duty to kill us, to beat us up and to accomplish certain objectives. But they had this type of security that was provided for them. If a detainee would try to hit any one of them or cause trouble in any way, then the security department, the security people would provide protection to those individuals who used to kill detainees. Nothing would happen to them. Do you understand what I am saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could I interrupt for a moment and try to clear up things. You said that the interrogators would come to the camp and go to the upper floor and that the interrogators would have contact with them. The interrogators would could contact with whom?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I'm referring to the office which I pointed a while ago, the office where the leaders were, where the commanders were.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, did you yourself ever observe the interrogators in that office conferring with the people who used that office?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: You mean if they talked?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes. Did you ever see them in that office --

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No, I didn't see them. I didn't listen. But, for example, I saw Drago Prcac with Meakic. They used to pass in the restaurant together, go for a beer and then come back. And there was an investigator who interrogated me, one of them who interrogated myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, when you would see Drago Prcac in the camp, what would he be doing?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Drago Prcac was always handling some kind of papers, some lists. I didn't see him doing anything special. He didn't walk around the compound very often, not at least in the area where we women were accommodated, where we could observe the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When was the last time you saw Drago Prcac in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: In Omarska, you mean? It was when he called our names from the list of women who were supposed to go to Trnopolje and those who were supposed to stay in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was that on your last day in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: On the 3rd of August, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you have also mentioned a person you call Krkan --

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: -- a person whose name you indicate you came to know while you were in the camp. How did you come to know who he was?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: It's not his name. This is how everybody called him. I don't believe there is such a name as Krkan. How I came to know him, was that your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: On that afternoon when Biba and I arrived, we were searched for weapons and taken to the kitchen where the rest of the women were. Then when the interrogators finished their work in those rooms where we slept, we were taken there for the first time. And Jadranka told me that in the morning I had to take my identity card with me and that I should go and see Krkan in the morning. And it was next door. We were separated by a corridor. I did as I was told. I took my identity card. I entered the room. He was sitting at a desk. I didn't know him, I just saw a big man. I gave him my identity card. In the meantime Jadranka had gone to make some coffee. And he had a very big notebook with him. It was a kind of register containing a number of names, numbers of identity cards, and so on. So he took my identity card and he took down my personal details. Then he looked at me and he came to me and he started to grab me, and that was the first thing -- the first time in my life that something like that was happening to me. I didn't know what was happening and I told him, "I'm an old woman," and he said, "Well, you're good. It doesn't really matter." So I was really shocked. But Jadranka entered the room in the meantime and we managed to go back to our room.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where was it that he started to grab you? On what part of your body?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: My breasts.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did he grab your breasts?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Something like that. My breasts, in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, other than this first instance when he grabbed your breast, did he ever assault you that way again in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Other than that instance when Krkan grabbed your breast, did anyone in the camp assault you sexually?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: From my room, you mean? My room?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did anyone assault you personally?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Not me. Me, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, after this first contact that you had with Krkan, did you have any personal contacts with him after that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How often?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: During my stay in the camp, one more time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what happened --

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No, not one more time. I'm sorry. But exactly twice. Exactly twice.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened on those two other occasions?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: He made it possible for me, through Prcac, to be taken to the garage to see my husband for a couple of minutes. And one other time, the women were so hungry, they were faint, they couldn't walk, and I ran out into the corridor and said, "Krkan, give us something to eat because these women here are going to starve." And Krkan said that when the dinner was over, and if there were anything left over, he would bring us something. And he did bring some food and a plate to the door and we took it inside and we ate it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, when you were in Omarska, how often would you see Krkan?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Whenever he was in the third shift, I would see him often in the corridor, on the way to the toilet; when we would go to the toilet, when we had to go. But we went out more often than that because we wanted to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In what corridor, in what building and on what floor?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: On the first floor, near our room, in the corridor when we moved around. Near the area where we slept. Not in the dining area, but upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, in addition to seeing him upstairs in the corridor of the first floor, were there any other areas of the camp where you saw him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Other areas in the camp where I saw him? I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see him in the room in which you slept?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How often?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Not very often, but I would see him there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When would this be? During the day or during the night?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: During the night.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you saw him in the room at night, what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: He would come to fetch Turkanovic, I think her first name is Sebiha, the owner of the Red Roses of Kozarac who was in my room.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Would he take her out of the room?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long would she be gone from the room?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I didn't really watch. I wasn't interested.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Would she return to the room that night, or would you not see her until the next day?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Sometimes she would come late.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When she returned, were you ever able to observe her condition?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No. It was night-time. There was no light so I couldn't see. And we didn't trust one another so we didn't discuss any problems amongst ourselves. We didn't even know each other well enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You also mentioned a person by the name of Krle that you, in your testimony indicated, was also a shift leader. How did you come to know Krle?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, I had occasion to talk to him often. It was in his shift that I would go upstairs to clean the rooms, and the toilet downstairs. And I'd ask him where he worked, and unless he lied, he told me he worked in the agricultural cooperative. And I feared him most.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How did you learn that his name or his nickname was Krle?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Everyone called him that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How often would you see him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Whenever he was on duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you said that it was on his shift that you would go upstairs to clean the rooms and the toilet downstairs. Who was it who would give you those duties?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Krle for the toilet, and for the rooms, I offered to do it myself, I volunteered.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: To whom --

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Krle. Myself and Advija Mahmuljin, the two of us would go to Krle.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And when you volunteered, to whom would you volunteer?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: To Krle.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know a person in the camp by the name of Zoran Delic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Extremely well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his ethnic group, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: He was a Serb. A Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where did he work in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: He was the head of the canteen, and he is from Gradina, a village called Gradina.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever observe him abuse detainees?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Every time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Every time what? When? When would that happen?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Every time when they would tell him from the gates that a new group of prisoners was arriving, then he would either clap his hands or something, and they would all gather and they would all start beating every one with planks, with fists, with legs. No one was spared. That is the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you a few questions about conditions in the camp while you were held in Omarska. How was food delivered to the detainees in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I would prefer to tell you, for all of you to gain insight into the situation, that this social canteen had been planned for an initial capacity of 150 persons. When it was turned into a camp, there were more than 600 people, plus those who couldn't come to eat they were so badly beaten up. And you don't need much to work out. The area is 18 by 11, and the time for a meal was three minutes, and if you know that there would be 30 people in one round, and if one hour has 60 minutes, then you will all be able to work out that 600 people had to eat per hour. So I called it a meal of death.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mrs. Cikota, how many hours a day would you serve meals to the detainees?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: How many hours? This would last -- it depended on how much beating went on. About four or five hours, I think. From around -- it wasn't always the same time because we waited for the food to arrive. About half past eight or 9.00 until 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you would start at 8.30 or 9.00 in the morning, and this would continue until 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, let me go back to my first question and ask you, how was food delivered to the detainees? By what type of vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: It was a small TAM truck, vehicle. It was always the same vehicle. I think it was yellowish in colour. I think two-tonne capacity, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What other uses, if any, was that truck put to?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I know because I saw it every day. In front of the left window, people who had been killed were transported to their burial place. They knew where. The people who had been killed were transported in that vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown, please, Exhibit 3/37. If that could be put on the overhead projector, please.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's exactly what it looked like, and those were the caterpillar tyres of a 75-tonne dumper.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So the picture of that truck is the truck that brought food and carried dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That may by returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: During the time that you were held at Omarska camp, how many times were you allowed to go outside the restaurant building?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I went out once because I had a visitor. An older man, an electrician who used to work in Omarska came to see me. His name was Dusko Dronjak. My sister and brother-in-law had sent him to see whether I was alive. And he entered freely, came to see me and said, "Let's go out," and we sat on a bench and I sat and talked to him for as long as I wanted. That was the one time I went out.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were outside, did you see a vehicle come into the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did this vehicle bring to the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: It brought food for our tormentors. It transported food.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see what type of food the camp personnel received?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the difference, if any, between the food that the camp personnel received and the food that was given to the detainees in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: There's no comparison at all. It's impossible to compare.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What type of food did the camp personnel receive?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Good quality food. Meat, cooked. We watched them eating tomatoes with our eyes wide open. You couldn't imagine eating it. Vegetables, nice sandwiches. We couldn't even see what they were eating because they ate out of sight, so we couldn't see. But we could see when they ate their sandwiches because they moved around, and once I was given a sandwich like that which I ate.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what was the sandwich? What kind of sandwich was it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: It was a wonderful sandwich with salami and butter. A very nice sandwich. It was pieces of bread rather than a bun. It was a very nice sandwich.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The water that the detainees drank in the camp, what was the quality of that water?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I'm really annoyed by that question. Surely you could have analysed that water by now. If you had taken a sample, you could have analysed it, and then you would know exactly what we drank. Our detainees drank spring water that was brought to them. I saw that because I once got a cup of that water. So I feel it's really unnecessary for me to talk about this. I don't believe in any stories. I believe in exact tests. And I know that technically, never was a permit for use issued for the water supply in the separation plant.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question. The translation I have indicates that the detainees drank spring water that was brought to them. Is that correct? Were detainees given spring water?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No. For heaven's sake, take a sample and see what we drank.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mrs. Cikota. Would you please answer my question? Were you detainees given spring water?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: It's not true. It's not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: All right. What kind of water were detainees given?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: It's shameful if anyone said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Ma'am, it was on the transcript. I'm asking you to correct it. So what kind of water did detainees get?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Industrial water.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, did you ever have occasion to drink the water that was given to camp personnel?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, once. My student gave it to me who was a policeman, in a tin cup, and it was wonderful water. Cool, fine. And we had to drink the water for industrial use, we detainees.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, this water that was given to you by your student, what kind of water was that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Beautiful water, cool. And I asked him where it came from, and he said, "It came from the spring, teacher."

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What effect, if any, did this industrial water have on you while you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: A terrible effect. When I urinated, it was red. I urinated blood. I personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, what time are we --

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Why don't you analyse the water yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. What time are we taking the break, at 11.00 as usual?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was thinking of having a break at twenty to eleven or just now, but I was trying to see whether you would finish or not with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We're turning to a new area, Your Honour, so it perhaps would be a good time to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So we're going to have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Madam Hollis, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mrs. Cikota, I would now like to ask you some questions about persons detained in Omarska camp. You've mentioned Jadranka Cigelj. What was her ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: She was a Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And was she active in politics in the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I think she was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what party, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: With the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You testified earlier about your involvement in the referendum. To your knowledge, did she have any function or involvement in that referendum?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what was her involvement, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I saw her at one of the meetings, when we took over some documentation for the elections, in one of the big rooms of the municipal housing department where all of the presidents were present. Braco Seric also attended the meeting. At the time he was the chairman of the election commission, and he gave us some instructions, some guidelines as to how to organise the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you've also mentioned that Velida Mahmuljin gave the opening speech at the SDA assembly.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you see her in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. She told me she was the first woman -- she had been the first woman to arrive in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, where is Velida Mahmuljin today?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: She stayed in Omarska after I had left, together with a group of five other women who were there for the needs of the committee, of the headquarters, and so far I haven't heard that she's still alive. I don't have any information about her.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know a woman named Jasminka Hadzibegovic before you were taken to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. She was a neighbour of mine. She used to live in the same house as Darko Prcac. She's a judge, lawyer. She used to work at the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What involvement --

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: And she was involved in election coordination.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In election coordination. What involvement, if any, did she have in the referendum?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No. Involvement? Her functions were in the main committee. If there was something that was unclear, if there were any problems, they used to have a number of telephone lines and she was in charge of coordinating things. So she was involved in that particular department for the elections.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And did you see her in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. I saw her together with -- and I saw her brother and her husband as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And they were in the camp as detainees?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know a woman by the name of Munevera Mesic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I used to know her husband very well because he used to be a manager of a factory, and I worked with him in the bank. As to Munevera, I came to know her in the camp. I didn't know her before. Her husband worked in the wood pulp department of the factory. And she was accommodated in my room.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, what was her ethnic group and the ethnic group of her husband?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: They were both Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And she was one of the women in your room at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, she was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know or come to know a woman by the name of Mugbila Besirevic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: She used to work with me in Privredna Banka. She was an economist. I used to know her from before. She was also in my room.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was she well known in the Prijedor area for her activities?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, she was, and that's why she was arrested. Apparently she had heard about the collection centres, and she attempted to collect food and help people, and that is how she was detained and taken to Omarska. I didn't see that, but that was the story. But, yes, she was active. And she was a very well-known person in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what was her ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall an incident that occurred in the dining-room involving Mugbila and Munevera?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I recall that incident. I recall it very well. Do you want me to talk about it?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Judges what happened?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: There was a front door in the restaurant, and a very tall young man, aged between 30 and 40, entered the restaurant through that door. Two very young women came. They were about 20 years of age, and they were very lightly dressed because it was very hot. They were wearing some kind of hot-pants. There was a counter there which separated us, and this man stood there for a while observing us. He was wearing some kind of gloves without fingers. He was dressed all in black, like a Mexican, and he wore a leather belt, and at his belt he had a knife. I think he had a pistol as well, but I'm sure he had a knife. So very slowly, gingerly, he approached us. We stood there. We didn't say a word; we were silent. Then he asked, "Which one of you used to work in the bank?" Then Mugbila answered I did. Then he said, "So you were giving loans to the area of Cazin." So he took out his knife and he carved a cross. I don't think it was very deep, it was just a surface cut. Munevera is an exceptionally beautiful woman, and she must have found a kind of overcoat in the room. She was trying to be unobtrusive. On that occasion she was wearing this blue overcoat. She has quite large breasts. At one point, this young man approached her and he said, "What would you think if I cut one of your breasts now?" She didn't say anything, and then after that, he left. We were petrified. We didn't dare look on. But later, when we came back to the room, we comment on the event.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: This young man that did this, did you recognise him as someone who worked regularly in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you see any camp personnel with him during this incident?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No. No. He was alone with two young persons, but they did not come closer. They remained where they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did any camp personnel intervene to stop this incident?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No. There were no interventions whatsoever if there was a beating or killing going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know a woman by the name of Edna Dautovic before you were brought to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, I did, because she has a house in the same neighbourhood where Kvocka's parents-in-law used to live, and I used to know her very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution would like to offer Exhibit 3/63.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Ma'am, would you please look at that photograph and tell the Judges if you recognise anyone in that photograph.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: This is Edna Dautovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So Edna Dautovic is the adult woman in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was Edna Dautovic's ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: She was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You can return that exhibit to the registrar, please. Did you meet a woman named Sadeta Medujanin the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall an occasion when both Edna and Sadeta were called out of their rooms?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that occasion very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And do you recall what, if anything, was said about why they were being called out?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall when it was that they were called out?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: In the evening hours of the day. Around 10.00 perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall how long you had been in the camp when this happened?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I must have been there for about a month, more than a month.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, what did you do after these two women were called out?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: When they called out people, they never actually entered the room. They would simply open the door but remain in the corridor. So on that occasion they said that Sadeta Medujanin should come out. We didn't have any things with us, so we left the room immediately. As she was leaving, she simply said, "I hope, ladies, that you won't hold anything against me."

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, after these women were called out, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I opened the door immediately and I went to the toilet, and I stepped on the toilet bowl and I observed a bus, and I saw them take their places on the bus, and they read out what was written, and it looked like an exchange. That's what they were told. They were told that they would be exchanged. We were very happy for them in our own, because we thought that it was good for them that they would be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, in addition to these two women, did you see any other individuals being loaded onto this bus?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: These other individuals, were they male or female?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: All males except for the two of them, and they were sitting at the front seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You indicated that you saw this from the toilet areas of the first floor of the administration building.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution would offer 3/104, which is a photograph of the model of Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Ma'am, I would ask you to look at this photograph of the model and then point to the area where you saw this bus on the night Edna and Sadeta were called out.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Just a second, please. I need my glasses. The bus was here, in the middle of this area, which means between the pista and the restaurant building, closer to this part here.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So as we look at the photograph, it was closest to the corner that is the left corner as you look at the photograph.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Ma'am, after these two women were called out, have you ever seen either one of them?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, are both of these women listed as missing today?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Most probably so.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you have testified that on some occasions Krkan came into your room and took out Sebiha Turkovic.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What other women, if any, in your room were called out at night?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Jadranka Cigelj, Sadeta Avdic. I think that Sadeta is her first name. Then there was also Suada. What was her last name? Ramic. And also Mirsada Hadzalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When these women returned to the room, were you able to observe their emotional or physical condition?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No. It was night-time and there were no lights. And also there wasn't any trust amongst ourselves. I mean, we didn't confess to each other, confide in each other. At least they didn't tell me anything. They may have told it to some other women, but I didn't have any contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to see any signs of bruising on any of these women?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: On Sadeta Medunjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What bruising did you see?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Those were not bruisings. What she had was some kind of blisters from cigarettes, cigarette butts, traces of cigarettes that had been put out in this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you some questions about some of the male detainees in the camp. Camil Pezo, Husein Basic, and Husein Crnkic, did you know these men before you came to Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Camil Pezo, yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And Husein Basic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Basic, yes. We are related.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And Husein Crnkic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Husein Crnkic, yes, I know him very well as well. I used to work in the school with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the ethnic group of these men?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did these men hold any positions in the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: As far as I know, they did; Husein Basic, Husein Crnkic, Camil Pezo as well. As regards Camil Pezo, he was an economist; Husein Basic, a lawyer; and Husein Crnkic, a maths professor. He used to work in the grammar school; he used to be the principal there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, what position did they hold in the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I believe that they were members of the executive committee.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You saw --

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I think they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And you saw them as detainees in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I observed them, I watched them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you saw them, what was their physical condition?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Very poor condition. Huso Crnkic spent all his time in the "white house." He didn't always show up in the restaurant to eat; he came on several occasions. He wore a chequered shirt, and as he would pass by me, he left it open on purpose so that I would see that both his clavicle bones were broken. So he thought that I knew about the situation and he would ask me about his brother, Esref, who was an engineer, and he was a manager of the maintenance department in the Omarska mine or company.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And was --

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: He was very famous as an engineer.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was Esref also in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, Nedzad Seric, Eso Mehmedagic, and Omer Karenovic, did you know those men?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Mehmed Seric, you said? Who else?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Nedzad Seric, also Eso Mehmedagic --

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I know all of these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was their ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: They were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did these men perform any function related to the referendum?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I think they did. This one is a lawyer, this one as well, and this is another lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So all three --

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: They were all lawyers.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: -- were lawyers. What was their condition when you saw them in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I saw Braco Seric only once, when he was taking his meal. He had lost a lot of weight. He had to be carried by two other men, like this. He was unable to walk.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And Eso Mehmedagic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Eso Mehmedagic, he used to live in the same building as Prcac so he was a neighbour of mine as well. He was a very intelligent man, but he had very poor sight. He underwent two surgeries in Russia. And his wife who used to work as a nurse in the health centre would take him to work and back home. He was in the camp and he was also led by Ibro Paunovic. Ibro Paunovic was an engineer, and he was a member of the executive board of the mining company in Ljubija; he was an expert in energetics. And he would be seen from time to time in the kitchen, and they teased him as being a sniper shooter. And he could barely walk. Once I asked about Eso and I was told that he had gone home.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Would you give me a moment, please. Who were they referring to as a sniper? Who?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Eso Mehmedagic, that he was a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You mentioned Ibro. What was his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Omer Karenovic, what was his condition when you saw him in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: He was also in a very poor condition. He was also a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know two men named Ado and Omer Ekinovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was their relationship to each other?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Ado was Omer's son.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was their ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: They were Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know a man called Slavko Ecimovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, and his wife Cica. She worked as a typist in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Slavko Ecimovic, what was his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: A Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did Ado Ekinovic and Slavko Ecimovic know each other?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. Slavko was the witness at Ado's wedding, Ado being Omer's son.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When did you last see Ado in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: The last time, on the 7th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: What did I see? Ado, Omer, Medunjanin's son, and Hajro Hodzic were members of the worst extremists group, and they were all the time detained in the "white house." Then Ado stayed in the "white house," one could see that at lunch, and Omer was moved to the garage. I saw, I think it was the 7th of July, after interrogation, Ado was thrown out. He was dead. And I saw Burho, a man from Prijedor, with a group of other men, they carried him to the left window of the "white house," near the left window of the "white house." The surname of Burho is Kapetanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When was the last time you saw Omer Ekinovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Omer also went once for interrogation. Again, he too was thrown out on the pista, and this same man, Burho Kapetanovic, with a group of other men, carried him to the same spot where Ado had been thrown. Just beneath the left window of the "white house," viewed from the restaurant building.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And when Ado and Omer were thrown on this spot near the "white house," did you see any signs of life in either body?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned Burho Kapetanovic. Did you know him before you came to the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
