utterances.text: Yes. Yes, well, both him and his brother Miho. Miho Kapetanovic is an economist, a manager, in Prijedor, whom I also saw in the camp. He's Buhro's brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Burho, what was his occupation?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: He was a craftsman. I don't know exactly. A metalworker of some sort, but I don't know his exact trade.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you say you saw him in the camp, what was his condition?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: You're talking about Burho?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: He was of heavier build. He wasn't fat, but he wasn't in as poor condition as compared to Ado, who was completely deformed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When did you last see Buhro Kapetanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I think it was the 26th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what did you see?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: He was taken away and after that I didn't see him again. He was taken together with Mujo, in a group, with Ziko's son and Ziko Crnalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And Mujo, who is Mujo?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: A man from Prijedor who was head of the garage in the sense that Jadranka Cigelj was head of our room. In that sort of sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And who was Ziko?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Ziko Trnolic and a caterer. And his son, they called him Caruga. I don't know his name. They all also related to my sister-in-law. They had a cafe in the same area in which Kvocka's mother-in-law lived, and they are closely related.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And Ziko and his son, what was there ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know a man named Ago Sadikovic before you came to the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I did well, because he is from my area and his wife comes from the same place as I did, and we lived across the street from one another, and we would meet often when we went to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was Ago Sadikovic's occupation?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I think he's a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was he held as a detainee in Omarska as well?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, in the "glass house."

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When was the last time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I think it was the 23rd of July, when he was taken away.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what did you observe on that day when he was taken away?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I watched him all the time. He had a leather jacket thrown over his left arm. He was wearing a short-sleeved shirt. They took him through the window and directed him towards the hangar. Then closer to the "white house" than the red one there was a vast reel with a coaxial cable for long distance transmission was wound onto, and behind this wheel of cable I heard two silenced shots, and they killed him there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you have testified that on the 3rd of August, you left Omarska. How many women remained behind when you left the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I think five.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Can you recall who that was?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Mugbila Besirevic, then Sebiha Turkanovic, Zdenka. How many have I mentioned? Sabiha Turkanovic, Zdenka, Mugbila, Hajra, and Velida Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, how many of those --

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: And these two were taken for exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, how many of these women you have just named remain unaccounted for today?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Hajra is unaccounted for, Mugbila. Sabiha and Zdenka survived. I know about them. And for the other three, they didn't leave Omarska. They didn't get out of Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where were you taken to from Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: To Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And how long were you held there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: About five days.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How were you able to leave Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: For us it was like paradise compared to Omarska, so that women would come, and in a group of women they escorted me to my house. We took a train, a passenger train -- there was a train then -- and then on foot to my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you went back to your home in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in your home in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: On the 23rd of January, 1993. Until the 23rd of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were the conditions like for you during the time you lived again in your home in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Impossible. We didn't have enough food. I didn't go out. There were threats, telephone calls; "What are you waiting for, you motherfucker? We're going to come and slit your throat." Things like that; very dreadful provocations. I would have tolerated all those provocations if I didn't have small children, if I had been alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you have to do to be able to leave Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I had to get some 13 certificates that I had no -- that I didn't owe anything to the bank, that I had never been convicted. I had to pay for the electricity, the telephone, and lots of other things. And after all these pieces of paper -- I got a piece of paper which I still have in my possession which says, "You may now leave the Republika Srpska." That is literally what it says. When you'd paid everything, that you have met all your debts, then you may leave Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you do with your property?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I entrusted all my property to Drago Prcac. Even his wife, I gave her a colour TV, a video recorder, and my kitchen and dining-room, and she gave me 500 marks for me to be able to leave Prijedor and to be able to pay all those bills. All my other property I entrusted to Drago Prcac.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you testified earlier that from 1985 until May of 1992 you were employed at the Privredna Banka Sarajevo. Did you receive a notice that your employment at the bank had been terminated as of 1 July 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. I was in the camp, and when I came home I received this, because for five days I hadn't come to work and I was fired. That was the reason for firing me. I have a document to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Why didn't you go to work for five days?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I was in the camp. How could I go to work?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The property that you had in Prijedor, have you regained that property?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And the financial and other assets that you had, have you ever regained those?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Have you ever received any payment for your property that you had in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court the psychological and emotional effects on you of what happened to you in Omarska and the conditions there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I don't know whether you will be able to understand because you were never in that situation. When I left the camp, I weighed 51 kilos.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you weigh before you went to the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Eighty-five, eighty-six. But it's not the kilos that are important. The food was dreadful, and because of a lack of salt and sugar the brain couldn't function properly. Then in Berlin, a friend of mine, who was treated by a well-known psychiatrist, took me there. So I was given eight tablets of magnesium a day and some special baths, and he treated me as if I was a child. I would have to draw a school, a school in his house, and I would have to jump over that, like hopscotch, and then a rope for me to skip with, skip over, as if I was a child. And so he stopped the car. I thought he was crazy and he thought I was. He said, "When you smile and when you start crying, then everything there be all right." I was simply petrified, turned to stone. I don't know whether you can understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mrs. Cikota, you have mentioned several personnel --

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I couldn't believe that such horrors could exist, that those were human beings. Wild animals wouldn't do that. Shame on anyone who does this.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mrs. Cikota, you have mentioned several people who worked at the Omarska camp. Realising that it has been eight years since you were in the camp, do you believe that today you would be able to identify these people which you have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Of course I could. Their pictures are in my mind every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mrs. Cikota, I would ask you to look around the courtroom, and if you see the man you referred to as Kvocka, could you please indicate where he is and what he is wearing.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: May I take this off?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would prefer you leave that on, please.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Shall I get up?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you need to. But stay, please, at your chair. If you don't need to get up, you may remain seated.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: You're asking me about Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Kvocka, next to Krkan. He has his headphones. I can only see his neck. Why don't you get up so I can see your shirt? He hasn't got a tie. He has a white shirt with a check on it, I think, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you said that Kvocka was next to Krkan. As you look at Kvocka, using your left and your right, is Krkan to his left or to his --

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: To his left. You see, there he is. Something in purple, a purple kind of tie and a white shirt. They know me. All these men know me very well, just as I know them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, you have also mentioned Prcac.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: After all, we were in the same place for 42 days. Prcac you want.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You also mentioned Prcac. Could you look around the courtroom and tell the Judges where he is and what he's wearing.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Prcac is writing something. He has glasses on. He's changed a little. He has a moustache. In those days he didn't have one. He has a grey suit with a tie, with some white print on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You also mentioned a person you referred to as Krle. Could you look around the courtroom and see if you recognise Krle in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Of course I know Krle. There's Krle. He has a blue tie. He has a different hairdo than he did then. What colour is his suit? Greyish, I think. They know me just as I know them --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And where --

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: -- and it's not hard to identify them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mrs. Cikota, where is he located?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: One, two, three. He's next to Kvocka, isn't he. Looking from this side. Krkan, Kvocka, Krle.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Hollis. Ms. Cikota, you are now going to answer questions put to you by the Defence attorneys. Mr. Krstic -- oh, sorry. Mr. Krstan Simic, in which order are you going to cross-examine this witness? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as we didn't have a break, then we will go in the order of the indictment, and if some counsel members have no questions, they won't. I will be the first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask them to introduce themselves, the people who are going to put questions to me, the way I introduced myself, with their full name and surname and all their references?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. You have the right to know, and I think they will introduce themselves, Witness, so just wait a minute. Thank you very much. Mr. Simic, you have the floor. You may begin, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mrs. Cikota --

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: May I have a piece of paper so I may note down your questions? Can I have a piece of paper? Just a moment, please, for me to put my glasses on. Thank you. I'm at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: As you heard from the Presiding Judge what my name is --

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I can't write with this. Can I get a pen, please? No, I don't remember it. Could you tell me your name?

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: My name is Krstan Simic, I'm an attorney from Banja Luka, and I represent Mr. Kvocka as his Defence counsel. I have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Fine. I'm listening.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: During your testimony you told us how you were a public figure; you knew many managers, many of whom you named.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So could you very briefly try and explain to Their Honours, the Judges, how, in the territory of Prijedor municipality, the appointment of managers and executives and officials was carried out. Of course we are talking about the period prior to these unfortunate events, prior to the war.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So please will you do that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Before the war, because I first worked in the economy so I am very familiar with that, 90 per cent of the managers were Serbs. If you want me to list their names from one company to another, who was the manager where, I can do so. Muslims held construction firms and the public utility company in Prijedor. I can tell you who was the general manager of the mine, of the transportation. I can give you all those.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who was the principal of the secondary school?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: The principal of the secondary or grammar school -- but that was after the elections. Husein Crnkic was the principal, but that was afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who was the director of the health insurance administration?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: But that is not the economy.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: We are asking about the institutions that were important for the system.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Of the SIS. My husband was the director of the health insurance administration, but that is outside the economy.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who was the director of the pension fund?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Why don't you ask me about the economy?

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I'm sorry, madam, I'm asking you about the pension fund. Will you please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: But I'm saying that's not the economy. Those are the social services. These are minor services.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You say minor services?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, minor posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who was head of the SUP or the public security station in Prijedor before the war? Of what ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: That was after the ethnic cleansing of Prijedor, not before the war. Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: But I have clearly asked you, in a language you understand, who was the head of the SUP prior to Hasan Talundzic, to make it simpler.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Before Hasan Talundzic, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you know someone called Mesic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Besic, he was the president of the municipality in Prijedor when I came to Prijedor in 1973 after my studies, and not in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who was the general manager of the bank?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Nisevic was director of the bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What was his first name?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: His first name, I have his signature, Milan Nisevic, living in Puharska.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Madam, let's now go back to a subject linked to the multiparty events. In the 1990s, did a party of reformists appear on the political scene in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who was the leader of that reform party?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Durakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I'm asking you a question.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No, no, let me speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I was the party secretary of the bank in the last term, and we organised a trip to Sarajevo, and I was present at the meeting in that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who was head of the party at the level of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: At the level of Yugoslavia? Why would I have to know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Have you heard of Mr. Ante Markovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, excuse me. Please answer the question, and don't give us an answer why should you know. Either you know it and you give us the name, or you don't know and you tell us you don't know, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know someone called Ante Markovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't get that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know someone called Ante Markovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: He is the man who was supposed to save Yugoslavia, but he didn't succeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was he head of the reform party?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: He wasn't present at the meeting in Sarajevo, the one I attended. Durakovic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Very well. What were the relations of the national parties towards the reformist party?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I was party secretary of the Prijedor bank, and I knew that Serbs were leaving the party and joining the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Madam, I am trying to ask very clear questions, and you are avoiding answers. I didn't ask you about your party membership. I wanted to know what was the relation -- what was the attitude of, for example, the SDS towards the party of Nijaz Durakovic, that is, the reform party?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I'm telling you, they were leaving the party in large numbers. I'm very well familiar with that fact. Many of them left it.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Is the communist party the same as the reformist party for you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: What exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: The communists and the reformists, whether they were one and the same party for you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Again, I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In your opinion, was the former League of Communists, of which you had been a member and that's the party I'm referring to, is it the same thing as the party of reformists led by Ante Markovic? Were they one and the same party?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I believe that the ideology was the same, that they had the same objectives, both of those parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Were nationalist parties attacking the party you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Mostly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You mentioned the referendum.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was it conducted by the same election commission as was involved or, rather, in charge of the election for the first elections, first multiparty elections that took place in 1990 in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Whether it was the same commission, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Were you involved in the election process, in the organisation of the elections, and in which part? I'm referring to the elections that took place in 1990.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: You mean the 1990 elections?

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you have the same function?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Were you involved in the same area in the elections and in the referendum?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, I had the same function. I was given official documents from the relevant authorities; I was given adequate materials. Those were not my first elections. I used to work as a party secretary, and it was a matter of routine for myself. I accepted it, and this is what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Which election unit were you involved with?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: The one that was organised in the area where I lived, at Pecani, in the local school building. This is how it was. You don't have to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I'm merely checking the transcript, madam. Mrs. Cikota, what territory was comprised by the election committee that you were a member of? I'm referring both to the election and the referendum.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Those were two separate issues. Which territory were you involved with?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I was involved with my neighbourhood, the area of Pecani, Pejici. It is a residential area. You know yourself what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Yes, I know it very well. However, the elections did not involve only several buildings. I'm interested in the territory that you were in charge of.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I'm telling you, it was the area of Pejici.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You mean Pecani?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, Pecani. The area of Pecani only. You can check it yourself in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to check that, Mrs. Cikota.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Well, you can do it. There are records of it in the municipal building. You have all the names of the residents of that particular area, and you have the names of the people who voted. This is not confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Ever since the beginning of this questioning, Mrs. Cikota, we have a problem. Please try to answer my questions in a precise way.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Well, I believe I'm doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How many members did the election commission of Pecani comprise?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Five. I was the president, and there were four other members.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who were those other four members who were involved with the work of the election and the referendum?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: It was Beba Alagic who was there. There was also Zgonjanin's brother's daughter, his niece. You know Zgonjanin very well. He's a Serb. And there was a private entrepreneur who was a member of the commission, an Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know their names?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Of course I know their names. I can tell you their names. I will bring you the relevant decision if you need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Madam, we're talking about the referendum.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, I am talking about the referendum. It was a five-member commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What was the turnout?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Sixty-four per cent for the referendum, for a sovereign and unified Bosnia. You can check it in all relevant documentation in the municipality of Prijedor. Those documents are still there; they have not perished.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: We are not talking about the documentation. I would like to know something about your election commission.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I told you, 64 per cent in the municipality of Prijedor. I'm referring to the municipality I was involved with, that is, the neighbourhood I was in charge of, the neighbourhood of Pecani.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What was the electorate body in the neighbourhood of Pecani?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I don't remember it precisely. We had lists of people, lists of residents of this particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mrs. Cikota, what was the turnout of the Serbs from that area?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: It was a very good turnout. Dr. Turic was amongst the first ones who showed up. He showed up in the early morning hours. There were many other people whom I knew. And Turic came first with his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you remember when Mrs. Jasminka Kvocka came to vote?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Well, she was not a resident of the area I was involved with.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You mean the area of Pecani? She lived there.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Well, then, she didn't come to the election. I know Jasminka very well. But it is only one person. I told you that the turnout was 64 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You are trying to explain the legality of the issue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please be asked to slow down for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: You can check the lists, and you can see the number of voters. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Very well, Madam Cikota. Let us turn to your arrival in Omarska. You said you came in a police wagon, in a paddy wagon. How many people were with you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Well, there were only two of us, two women.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: On that day, Mrs. Cikota, after your arrival, did any other woman arrive, was brought to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When you arrived, who received you in front of the restaurant? Who was there to wait for you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Who received us? They searched us. We were not received. They searched us for weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who was the person who did the search?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: It was Strika. Strika was the one who came to my apartment and took me from my children who were minors at that time. He was there. He came to my apartment with another man whom I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: But I'm referring to the security personnel. Was there anyone from the security personnel when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: What kind of security personnel are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Well, you described them that way?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: They were not providing security for us, they were providing security for people who came there to beat us. MR. K. SIMIC: Mr. President, it is impossible to establish proper contact with witnesses. The witness is avoiding answers -- is avoiding my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I think you have to slow down. The interpreters are having problems with the speed. You have to make breaks. You have to pause between question and answer. I should like to ask the witness to answer questions in a direct manner, and I also should like to ask the counsel to ask clear and direct questions. Please try to let the witness answer your question. Wait a little before you ask another question, because if you yourself interrupt the witness, the witness doesn't have time to -- cannot answer your questions properly and clearly enough. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When did you arrive in Omarska, Mrs. Cikota?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: On the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: On the 23rd, who was present in the area where the police wagon stopped?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Who was present there? Beba and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I'm referring to the official personnel, official security personnel from Omarska.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Strikan was present there, Rade who had come to my house and had taken me to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Strikan, was he a member of the security personnel in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I know Strikan as a policeman. I know him from before. He used to work as a policeman in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Thank you. But what I want to know is whether any of the policemen were present there, any of the policemen who used to work in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Thank you very much. During your testimony, you mentioned a person by the name of Zeljko Meakic.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you know him from before, from before the war?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You also mentioned a policeman who was a member of the security personnel and who used to be your student.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. There were two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Could you tell us their names?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Boro Banovic was one of them. He worked there as an interrogator. The other one was -- I'll remember his name. I know that his uncle was -- just a second. He was very tall, blonde. He used to work with the police in Omarska. I will remember his name. I used to be his teacher. Bojic. Bojic was his name. A very tall young man.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know what Mr. Meakic was before the war? Do you know what his profession was?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No. I never seen him before.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You mentioned and you also recognised Mr. Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What was his occupation before the war?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I don't know. I know him by sight. I know his family, I know his wife, but I really don't know. I know that his wife was a seamstress and she used to work at the Pobjeda factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mrs. Cikota, thank you very much. I have no other questions for you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Simic. Mr. Nikolic, are you going to take the floor now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. This Defence team will not have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Fila. Let me just check one thing. Mr. Tosic, do you also have questions for this witness? This is just to know whether we're going to have a break now or not. Do you have any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our Defence team will not cross-examine this witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Tosic. Mr. Jovan Simic, you have the floor. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We will have questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. Mr. Fila, you may proceed. Sorry for this interruption. I just wanted to know the order so that we can organise our work in terms of breaks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once again -- I apologise -- I need to know whom I'm talking to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will do so, Mrs. Cikota. Witness, I told you at the beginning that each Defence counsel will introduce himself. So I can assure you that Mr. Fila will introduce himself to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Ms. Cikota, I'm Mr. Toma Fila. I am an attorney-at-law from Belgrade, and together with my colleague, Jovanovic, we are representing Mladjo Radic, or Krkan, as you yourself refer to him. My questions will hopefully be very brief, and I should like to have brief and clear answers from you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You spent two days in the Prijedor SUP before your departure?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you interrogated during those two days?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you searched? Were any documents taken from you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you left from Omarska the way you arrived.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No. I first went to SUP and then to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, but then from the SUP you went to Omarska, the same way you arrived there initially, with your documents, with all your possessions?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said you were accommodated in room B1, that you spent your nights there.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How often did you go to room B5? That's the room across your room where you saw Krkan.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Well, I went there very often. I went to see Drago, and I also used to clean those rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm referring to room B5.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I understand. I understand. I went there very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you see a radio station there? Did you see a telephone in that room?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who was working there? Who was involved with that radio station and the telephone?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Well, this was very close to our room. We could hear everything. We were sitting behind the door, so we were in a position to hear the conversations, but I couldn't tell you exactly who it was who specifically worked there, to be frank, but we used to listen to their conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said when you came in you gave your identity card.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And then after that your colleague Mrs. Jadranka went away to make some coffee. Did she indeed make coffee? Did she come back with the coffee?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I believe she did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you drink that coffee?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, who did she make the coffee for?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Mladjo grabbed me and I was totally confused, and I really don't remember what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You spent 42 days there in total?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you ever alone with Krkan?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: With Mladjo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did he attack you? Did he assault you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No, he didn't, but I think that it was because of Prcac. When he arrived, I was no longer afraid of anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is this what you think or do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I don't have any knowledge about that, but those were my feelings. That is how I felt at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You showed us a truck that used to bring food. Where was the food brought from?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: It was brought from the central kitchen, which was in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was that the place where the food was prepared even before the war?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I know all those places, because I used to work there. That is the same place where the food was prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did the guards have anything to do with the preparation of the food?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No. They had nothing to do with that. The food was prepared outside, and it came to Omarska in boxes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who was on that truck which was used to bring food? What persons were there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: What persons, what individuals? I don't know them, but I'm sure I could recognise them if I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I didn't ask you to identify them, I just wanted to know whether they were guards, whether they were employees of the mine.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of functions they had. They were dressed differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But they didn't have police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was any food prepared in the restaurant where you were?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No. No. The food was brought in already cooked.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You mentioned the issue of water. You said that you had had an opportunity to visit these buildings that were part of the Omarska mine company.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I used to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Near the restaurant, were there any fountains, any taps?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, there were. This is where we used to wash dishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you now tell me whether the water was from the waterworks?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there any water that was coming out from the taps?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was tap water, but I don't know whether it was drinkable or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please be specific in your answer, Mrs. Cikota?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Well, I'm doing my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As regards the water taps, do you know whether they had been in use even before the camp was open?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was it the same kind of water that was running through those taps?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So this is the kind of water that under -- that you say was not good for drinking, and it was also used before the opening of the camp.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Well, I should like to ask that analysis be made of this water.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The Prosecution is in charge of this analysis, not us. You mentioned the room B11. It was dark, there was no lights during the night?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that you had seen Krkan in that room in the dark.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I used to see Krkan very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where exactly did you see him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I would see him either in his office, in our room. Krkan was all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm referring to night-time, and I'm referring to your room specifically.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. Krkan was on duty during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was he on duty in your room as well?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm trying to ask specific questions, Mrs. Cikota. Please try to give specific answers. Did you see Krkan inside of your room in night-time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why and where exactly would you see him? Why would he come there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Well, he went -- he came to see Sabiha. She was the owner of Crvene Ruze.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, witness Mrs. Cikota, you are here for us. We need to understand you. If you speak too fast, then your efforts will be wasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My question is: When you saw this at night, you said that he came because of this Sabiha. Did he stay with her or did he just come to see her?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: He would call her and take her out, take her with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would he shut the door behind him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Our door was always closed. He would open it and close it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How did you know where he took her?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In front of your door, was there a guard during the night?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I didn't notice one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you had freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. We could go to the toilet and back. We were able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But you couldn't leave the building.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You mentioned a name Mitraljezac, the machine-gunner. Who was he in relation to room number 18 -- 11? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: There was another room, then the corridor where the table and chairs were. So he was in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does that mean that there were guards in the corridor?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: He was the machine-gunner who was watching over the whole pista with his gun pointed there, but he would sometimes come inside and have a cigarette with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I think that you said that there was another man sitting there in addition to the machine-gunner.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No, I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I misunderstood then. You use the word "exchange." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: That is what they told us. Prcac, for instance, would say, "They're going to be exchanged," or Krkan would say that. For us, that meant that -- do you mean how I -- what I understood it to mean at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What does "exchange" mean? What was being exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Men for men; people for people. Probably Serbs for Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So those who were leaving your camp were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: That is what they said. They simply said that they were going to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that you were able to see the "Red House" as well.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there any wire there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: In front of the "Red House"? I don't remember. That's quite far. It's not as close as you think and not as clearly visible, but I don't remember any wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know where coffee was made up there when Jadranka went to make coffee?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I didn't have access there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was it in the same room or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Since you've said that you knew quite a number of detainees, did you know somebody called Idriz Mujkic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Fila. Mr. Jovan Simic, it's your turn. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as my colleague Masic will be doing the cross-examination, are we going to have a break now or after our cross-examination? Because I'm afraid that we will not be able to finish as quickly as we usually do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that is preferable. Thank you very much for your suggestion. I was hoping we could release the witness, but perhaps there will be Ms. Hollis again, and the Judges' questions. So it's better to have a break. So we are going to have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. We are going to resume the cross-examination now by the Defence of Mr. Prcac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Cikota. My name is Dusan Masic, I'm an attorney from Belgrade, and I am a member of the Defence team of Mr. Drago Prcac. With me is attorney Jovan Simic who is also an attorney from Belgrade. First of all, I should like to ask you, before the 23rd of June, did you know anyone of the Prcac family except for Ljubisa Prcac?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: In your testimony today, you said that you established contact with the wife of Mr. Prcac before going to the camp to learn about the fate of your husband.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, by phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: So you called her up by phone.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, how did you look upon the Prcac family? Did you see them as friends?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, as friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: While you were at the camp, did you get food from Drago Prcac? Did anyone else bring you some food?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. Drago Prcac sent me a sandwich through a woman called Jadranka, and I don't remember anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: So no one brought you food sent by Prcac's wife except Drago Prcac.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: She sent food to my husband who was in the camp a month before me, but not to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: So she didn't send you any food.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No, I didn't need it when Drago was in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: What does that mean? Does that mean that you were given food while Drago was in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No. But I said that Drago, two or three times, I think two times, gave me food.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Did Drago bring you anything else except food?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: A winter fur coat that he brought from the house, from my children, which I wore and used as a cover. So he brought me my fur coat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Nothing else?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I don't remember. But I do remember this black fur coat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer anyway. During those 42 days of your detention, you said you spoke to Drago Prcac frequently. How frequently? Could you give us an indication? Every day, every other day, every third day?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: When he was on duty, I knew when he would come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: What did you discuss?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but can you tell me, what did you discuss?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Nothing important. I just begged him for me or my husband to survive because of the children. That was all we discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything about your children?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you that he was taking care of your children?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: So while you were in the camp --

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know what I'm going to say. Make pauses, please. Otherwise we can't follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, then, that Mr. Drago Prcac assisted your children as far as he could, because after all, there was a war on while you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, and even when I left the camp too. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: So Drago Prcac helped your family even after you left the camp.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: You said that you frequently sat and talked with Drago Prcac. In your opinion, madam, could Drago Prcac release you from the camp? Could he have said, "Zlata, go home"?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Do you think he could or not?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: During your testimony you mentioned Mr. Zeljko Meakic.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Zeljko Meakic Drago Prcac's superior?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I think that all three had the same function, both Drago and Kvocka and Meakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: How, then, do you explain that in your book, which you showed us when you entered the courtroom, you wrote that Kvocka and Drago Prcac were deputy commanders? I had the honour to read your book and that is what I read in it.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Those are judgements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: So you judged that they were deputies, in your judgement. Did you, in your book, assess their position as being deputy commanders?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I still maintain what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: So what you wrote in the book is not true?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Well, I have other information now, and I have a different understanding of things than immediately after leaving the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, then, that upon leaving the camp, you had the information that Prcac was a deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I still maintain that both Kvocka and Meakic and Drago Prcac performed the same duties and that they were commanders of the security of the investigative centre, of the concentration at Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Can I say, then, that you incorrectly stated in your book that they were deputy commanders?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I didn't have enough scope, enough access to documents about all of them. But over 42 days, that was my impression, and I think that the truth is what I just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Did you have access later to any documents? You said you didn't have any documents then, but later on did you have access to any documents on the basis of which you can came to the conclusion that you conveyed to us today?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No, no documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to anyone, and then on the basis of that conversation came to this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: As I consider myself a well-educated woman, I'm not an uneducated woman, so probably I have something in my own head so that I can draw my own conclusions from what I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. I had no intention to question your education or intelligence. My question is, your conclusion that Drago Prcac was deputy commander, did you change that conclusion due to anything except thinking it over?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No. I still claim that they were on a par.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher to show the witness document 3/104. It is a Prosecution document. The witness used it a moment ago so I should like to clear up a point.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Madam Cikota, we will be talking about the case when Sadeta Medunjanin boarded the bus and left for an exchange. You said today that you watched all this from the toilet window, so that is correct. That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Can you show us precisely or can you draw the position of the bus as you saw it? Could you do that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that allowed, please? Can the witness make an indication on the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if they mark on that exhibit, they will, in effect, be creating a new exhibit. We would ask that they use their own copy of that exhibit and mark it as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And do you have your own copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President, but in my copy, I have already drawn in lead pencil what the witness has pointed to, but -- just a moment, please. A minor technical problem. We'll deal with it quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number of this new exhibit will be D3/5.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I've drawn it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: I can see that, but I apologise, I'm afraid it's disproportionate in relation to the building, but never mind. So actually, the door to the bus, where was the door?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Just like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: What do these two lines mean?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Nothing. I drew it too much forward. So this is the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Where was it facing? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: It was facing in that direction. The driver would be up here, and this is the back part of the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. I do apologise. Were you looking through a closed window or an open window?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: An open window.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: How do those windows open?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I think to the right, with a handle. With a handle, to the right, facing the window from the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Let's be quite precise. Do those windows open from the left to the right and can they be opened wide?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: These are small windows, not big windows. Then there was upper part to that window, a second pane. There were two panes, two parts to the window. But regardless of that, one could see through the glass. It isn't important whether it was open or closed. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Did Drago help any other women?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: In his building, Zuhra or Zumra -- Drago can help me -- lived. Her surname is Mehmedagic. She lived in the same building as Drago. And when Drago entered the room, Zumra hugged him and said, "For God's sake, Drago, what am I doing here?" That was when Drago came into our room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Did Drago assist Zumra?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Zumra is a pensioner. She worked in the electrical ceramic combine. She came towards the end, so I didn't really notice. I don't know how many days she spent there, but she came close to the closing of the camp. But she lived in the same building. We're all neighbours. We lived close. And I think he brought her some clothes to put on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what Drago told Zumra in response on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: You said today that upon leaving the camp and before leaving, I think you said the 1st of December or the 1st of January 1993 --

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No, no. The 23rd of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Never mind. Let's be precise. You said that you left all your property to Drago Prcac.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Did Drago ask for that property?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: So will you explain to the Court how you left it to Drago Prcac?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: We signed a contract listing all the property. Drago got a copy of our property. We kept another copy of this, a copy, and both I and Drago have copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: As you said, and of course I know you are an educated woman, what is it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: It is a contract, a contract about the apartment, a contract about the garage, about our weekend home, our car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you what kind of a contract. Is it a gift? Did you leave it in his trust?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. I left it in trust.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: And by that contract you left Drago Prcac your apartment, your weekend home, your car, and your garage?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: What happened to the car?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: When we came back -- we went by bus to Gradiska, and when they turned us back or brought us back from Gradiska to Prijedor, they wouldn't let us cross into Croatia. They said we were extremists and that we had been in the camp, so they turned us back. We came back to the apartment. Then we told Ljubisa to tell his father to give us back our keys, and Ljubisa did bring the keys, and with that car we left via Banja Luka through -- with the help of Merhamet or I don't know what, and we crossed into Croatia. That's how it was exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that Drago Prcac returned your car as soon as you asked him to do so?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Madam Zlata, did you or any one of your family ask Mr. Prcac to return to you the property you entrusted to him, what is left, the apartment, the weekend home, and the garage?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Knowing the situation in Prijedor and following developments, not a single Muslim has returned to Prijedor yet, or are conditions such in Republika Srpska for Muslims to return, because the security situation is not such that we can live there normally and for us to be protected, and that is the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: That was not my question. My question was whether you ever asked for that property to be restored to you. However, in response to what you've said, a Muslim candidate participated as an independent candidate in the elections in Prijedor quite recently. Do you know who is the vice-president of Prijedor municipality? You don't know that he is a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: May I say something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. I'm sorry for interrupting you. Mr. Masic has asked you a question, a very concrete question, Madam Cikota. Please answer that question. Since your release, did you ever ask Mr. Prcac to give you back your property? That is the question.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: What do you think? Would Mr. Prcac return your property if you asked for it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I think he would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Your weekend home, was it destroyed before you left Prijedor? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Just one more rather technical question. You said today, madam, that you gave Mrs. Prcac a TV set and a video recorder, and she gave you 500 marks for you to be able to leave Republika Srpska to go to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. And I also gave her my dining-room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Do you think that in those days the value was proportionate to the assets?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I needed the money to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: But can you evaluate the value of the things that you gave? Were they worth more than 500 marks? I am thinking of the market value, not what those things meant to you personally.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Those were valuable things because all I had was of good quality, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just ask you something else at the end, personally. Would you have survived the Omarska camp if it hadn't been for Drago Prcac?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Out of the question. I'm quite convinced of that. Maybe I would have, but I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you: Did Drago have any reason to assist you except because he was the man he was?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I don't know, but after all, his son and my son were great friends. And he's a father, just as I'm a mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: So he did so because he wanted to help the parents of his son's friend.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Masic. Ms. Hollis, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Three questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You mentioned, in response to one of the questions on cross-examination, that at one point accused Prcac sent you a sandwich through a woman Jadranka. What was the last name of this woman Jadranka?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Jadranka. Who could remember all those names? She was fair, a fair young woman. I know she was Serb and she was not with us in our room, but I cannot remember her surname. Jadranka.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You were also asked about the first floor of the restaurant building and about a table and a chair that were in the hallway of the first floor of the restaurant building.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would ask at this time that the witness be provided with an exhibit which has been marked as 3/44A.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Ma'am, the picture that shows the table and chair, is this where the table and chair would be located that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was it that would sit at that table?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: We would call him Mitraljezac or machine-gunner. I don't know him but we women called him "the Mitraljezac."

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If that exhibit could be removed and if the witness could be provided with Exhibit 3/82. If that could be moved a little bit more so that the small red building is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, also during cross-examination you were asked about a building called the "red house." Could you show us on this exhibit where this building called the "red house" is located?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Hollis. Judge Fouad Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mrs. Cikota, good morning. I would like to ask you a few questions, and without going into details, I would like to have your impressions or your answers. Now, I gathered that you mentioned in your book that Prcac, Mr. Kvocka, and Meakic were deputy commanders and, judging by what you told us today, they seemed to have been the commanders. Now, based on your lively observation, your first-hand observation, who was the decision-maker in this camp? Who were the decision-makers there? Call them commanders or call them anything.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Who made the decisions, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good. Now, when you told us today that they were commanders, did it mean that they could be obeyed? They could give orders and could be obeyed?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Could they stop something from being done, somebody from being tortured, somebody from being killed, or vice versa, for them to be killed or tortured.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: They could have done all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: They could have done all that. You gave us the example of this tall, young man who came from outside with a knife and threatened Mubila, to cut her breast after wounding her and so on. There was nobody to prevent him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No, they didn't prevent anyone or protect anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But they could have?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: They could have, yes. That's the worst part of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What was the hierarchy of the others, of Krle, Delic, Krkan? Were they on a lower level from Prcac, Meakic, and Kvocka? Were they subordinates? Was it obvious?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: They were subordinate. They came by buses, and they were shift leaders and brought with them whole busloads of our torturers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I mean did they receive orders from higher up, from Prcac? You are sufficiently linked. You saw that Prcac could tell them, "Do that," "Don't do that," as well as Kvocka and Meakic? Or were they their own masters of the situation?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: They were all linked together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mean they were all one team, at the same level, the same standard.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, the other question is: When you said you were in the dining room, you could see the pista. Do you recall what was going on in the pista during the time that you were looking?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No one prevented us from looking. We could look all day. The pista and the "white house," everything was open to view. We spent all day there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What did you see, in short? If you want to describe it in a few words.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Just one example or several examples?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Well, give us several.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Several. But let me mention one in particular. I'll give you a few. One boy came in a police van. His name is Nisvet Suljic. The police van stopped between the dining room and the "white house." That young man was stocky, in his 30s. They immediately let him off towards the "white house." That young man turned around and hit the guard with his fist, the guard who was escorting him to the "white house." And he said, "Bosnia, don't give in," and he said it so loudly everyone could hear. It was lunchtime. All the guards who were in the dining room rushed out, and in front of the "white house," at the door of the "white house," they killed that young man, which means that all this was organised. I saw it with my own eyes. That is one small example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Okay. Other examples, you mentioned Husein Basic who was a professor of mathematics, and you could see the bones of his chest broken. Were some people chosen more than others for torture, and why? He was a professor of mathematics. Was there any reason for the choice?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Not only Basic, but all the intellectuals that I knew through the work I did were tortured and killed in a similar fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So the intellectuals were chosen first; is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Exactly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned that you never knew anything about being other than Yugoslav. You said that you were a Yugoslav until you went to Omarska camp. You didn't even know that you were a Bosniak Muslim. When did you realise that there was discrimination? Before you went to the camp, was life between the various factions without any discrimination?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. I learnt I was a Bosniak, a Muslim, when I arrived at the camp. I still have a colleague, whose name is Ljubinka Jakupovic and who was director of the foreign exchange department in the bank, with whom I have regular contact. We hear each other and see each other. But unfortunately what happened happened. Ljubinka is not to blame, nor am I, for what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So everybody had a mutual understanding and congeniality.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't even know the difference -- I couldn't tell by the names who was a Serb, who was a Croat, who was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned that when they arrested you, they accused you of being a fundamentalist. That was the translation we received.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Why did they think that? What was it based on? Why were you considered a fundamentalist, and what did they mean?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I don't know what they meant. But when I had this visit in Omarska, he told me that he had been at the SUP. His name is Dronjak. He said, "For Cikota, there is nothing on this document. I went to SUP. But as far as you are concerned, you surprised me. I am surprised to learn that you are a fundamentalist. I've known you for years, that you are an extremist, that you are took part in the armed attack on Prijedor."
