I didn't want to respond to that at all, so I said, "Well, if that's what they say, let it be." Then I realised that Dronjak was telling the truth because these investigators who came regularly to interrogate and torture Muslim people up there -- most people were finished from the beatings by these investigators -- I could see from their questions that these questions coincided fully with what this man, this electrician, told me, the one who came to visit me. Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Well, I just noticed what you said about the interrogation. You said before that Prcac and Meakic and Kvocka used to do the interrogation and that they were --

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No, I never said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: -- that they were the commanders, and in the upper room, that's where the interrogation was taking place. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I said upstairs, yes, but not in their offices. In the offices in which we slept, that is where the inspectors from Prijedor came.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, to one of the questions which has been asked of you by Defence counsel concerning Mr. Prcac, you answered that, "I would not have survived --" that you thought you would not have survived if he was not there.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: No, because of the allegations. All of the people who were members of the party, I mean all of the intellectuals were killed, and I was probably considered to be an intellectual so I would have probably been killed as other women. I don't know. It's just a feeling that I have. I think that if it had not been for Drago, I would not have survived. That is my belief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Can other people say the same thing, or were you the only privileged one, do you think? Would other people have survived thanks to him too?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: I don't know that. All I can tell you is about myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said you would have been killed like other women. So women were being killed too.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I would have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Riad. Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Ms. Cikota, I just want to make sure I understood some of your testimony earlier. Am I right that you said that the investigators would come in from outside and they would go to the upper floor, and names would be called out? Then I think you said that beatings would take place and they could do anything they wanted, and you said, I think, correct me if I'm wrong, that the shift commanders were subordinate to those people, and I think you used the words, or at least I have them in my notes, "the shift commanders were torturers." Now, I'm just trying to understand. Did you mean that the actual beatings took place by the interrogators and the shift commanders just didn't do anything about it and that's why they were torturers, or that the shift commanders themselves committed torture on prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Those people who came with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: In the bus, from outside.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you understood me correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So those were the people that, in your view, did the beatings and the abuse, and the shift commanders just didn't do anything about it and that's why you called them torturers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: They were all torturers, because anyone could do what they pleased in the concentration camp, even people who came from the outside. They were allowed in the camp. They were allowed to call out people, whomever they wanted, to kill anyone they wanted, to beat up people. This is how it went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: When you say that, are you still talking about the interrogators or do you mean some of the outsiders were allowed to come in and abuse the prisoners even if they weren't interrogators?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand you now, I think. My second question is: When you concluded your testimony, you said, very movingly, that you couldn't believe some of these people were human beings and that they behaved like wild animals. In your conversations with Mr. Prcac, since he was behaving in a friendly fashion toward you, did you ever discuss with him why he was taking a position of leadership in this camp where these things were going on or why he couldn't do anything to help the prisoners more than they were being helped?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: We couldn't discuss those things. It was never a subject matter. I feel grateful to him, but such conversations couldn't take place. We were just trying to figure out who would be killed next. There wasn't any conversation, properly speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Cikota, there was a question which reappeared on several occasions, and I should like to go back to that question again. You're an intelligent person, you're an educated woman, but could you please try to answer my question in an objective, unbiased manner, and tell me, what exactly was it that you saw, heard, or observed that led you to conclude -- to make conclusions as to the positions of the persons mentioned here, Kvocka, Prcac, and Zeljko Meakic? I'm not interested in your conclusions properly, just tell me exactly what it was that you saw or heard or observed that made you reach such conclusions, like a camera?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Well, I have told you this story about what had happened on one occasion in front of the "white house," for example. There are a number of such stories, and I don't think we should waste time on them. My impression was simply that all these people had a duty not to protect us but to kill us. However, if anyone should try to oppose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry to interrupt you, Mrs. Cikota. We shouldn't waste our time. I did not ask you why he was there. I simply wanted to know what you saw with your own eyes or heard with your own ears which allowed you to conclude that he was the commander or not.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: They were commanders. I saw a bus, for example, that used to come every day carrying investigators, inspectors, and they would pass by the window and they would go upstairs. They were the ones who interrogated people in our rooms. We would take our things and we would be in the kitchen while --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mrs. Cikota, for interrupting you, but we are now speaking about Kvocka, Prcac, and Zeljko Meakic. Why did you conclude that they were commanders?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Well, everybody addressed them that way. They had a Mercedes, they had drivers. So I don't know. That was my impression. Everybody would go to them. Everybody would contact them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. This is your impression, but you do not know exactly what led you to that conclusion, to that impression.

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Well, I was there and I could observe things for 42 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. Maybe this is a good beginning for this conversation. What was it that you observed during those 42 days that led you to conclude that they were commanders? What exactly was it that they did? What did you see them do?

utterances.speaker: ZLATA CIKOTA
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see them often. However, I saw people who had been beaten up, people who were very weak in the kitchen. I realised that some people were missing. I was watching people. I was observing people. However, I didn't see them kill anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. We should perhaps stop here. Mrs. Cikota, you have just completed your testimony here. Thank you very much for coming here. We wish you a pleasant journey to your place of residence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I have a question. I apologise. I have a question. Brenda, Brenda -- I'm sorry. I'm sorry, Your Honour. I have to. I haven't finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, madam. Witness Mrs. Cikota, you probably know very well what the procedure is. You know that the Judges are in charge of conducting the procedure. What is it you want to say? Could you tell me the subject, what you wanted to say, what you wanted to raise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a compensation claim, Your Honour, a compensation claim for the property that I lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please do so. You can tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall be very brief. I will mention only a few things. First of all, my personal income for the period as of the 1st of July 1992 until the 31st of December, 2000; second, the funds for the pension fund for the same period, for the same period of time; thirdly, compensation to the Socialist Republic of Germany Landsamt, for the social benefit and the utilities that -- payment of rent for the period from the 1st of April, 1993 onwards for my family; fourthly, compensation for fear, pain, and suffering because of the family members that were killed, friends and relatives. I am suffering permanent consequences because of that fear. I have been ruined. I am a traumatised, ruined person. I am not capable to work any more and to make any livelihood. Fifth, compensation for my cottage house in the village of Pejici, in the vicinity of Prijedor, which was completed in 1991 and subsequently destroyed; sixth, a three-room apartment which was built in 1980 in Duro Pucar Stari street, house number 56, the total area of it being 79 square metres, which I will not be able to use because I'm not allowed to go back to the area. I don't dare to go back to the area because of the security situation, however, in spite of the fact that legal provisions provide for that return. Seven, privately-owned garage in the vicinity of the above-mentioned apartment; eight, furniture from the living-room, furniture from the bedroom, from the nursery, and furniture from the kitchen and the hall, including carpets. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that all, Mrs. Cikota?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have questions? We will first release the witness perhaps. Mrs. Cikota, thank you very much once again for coming here to the Tribunal. The usher will now escort you and you will leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic, you wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much for this opportunity, but maybe this is beside the point now. However, as regards this compensation claim, I should like to tell the Court that I was empowered by Serbian victims from the Celebici camp to represent them, and I should say that we had no opportunity whatsoever to submit a compensation claim. I just wanted to say that I support what you just did, although, again, as I said, this is maybe now beside the point. I don't think there are any procedural possibilities for such compensation claims anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic, thank you very much for raising this issue. I believe that you understand that sometimes victims find themselves in such a situation that they simply have to express themselves. So we have to bear in mind the three objectives of this Tribunal, and that is the administration of justice, the restoration of peace in the area in question, and that we also need to give an opportunity for the victims to express themselves. But you know very well that the Tribunal does not have enough resources to go beyond that and to do something specific in terms of compensation claims. When I allowed this witness to speak about her compensation claim, it was in the spirit of the work of this Tribunal which has to enable victims to express themselves. You know probably that the Statute of the Permanent Criminal Court has a provision for this issue, but we do not have it. I hope that you understand that this has been a kind of homage to the victim and that we wanted to give the witness an opportunity to speak. But thank you once again for raising this issue. I hope you understand what we did. Ms. Hollis, I don't think we have enough time to start with our next witness. It is five to two.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, we could deal with the exhibits that were offered during the testimony of this witness. If that's permissible, I will indicate the exhibits that the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: -- offers. Your Honour, we had offered into evidence exhibit marked 2/1.1. That is a map of the opstinas in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We also offered into evidence 3/44A. That is a photograph of the first floor of the administration building, the hallway near the stairwell, with a table and chair. We also offered 3/44A [sic]. That was a photograph of four individuals, the one adult. I'm sorry, Your Honour, if I've misspoken. 3/44A is the photograph of the hallway. 3/63 is a photograph of four individuals. The one adult in that photograph was identified as Edna Dautovic. 3/103 is a photograph of a model of the Omarska camp showing the restaurant building from the side nearest to the grass and the "white house." It shows the dining-room area. 3/104 is a photograph of a model of the Omarska camp that shows the restaurant building and the pista from the side of the restaurant building where the offices are located. This was used in direct-examination in regard to the bus onto which Sadeta Medunjanin and Edna Dautovic were loaded. The Prosecution would again offer those exhibits into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Hollis. Let us hear the Defence. Could we have a spokesperson on behalf of the Defence? It seems that Mr. Masic would also like to tender something into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to tender into evidence the photograph which was marked by the registrar D3/5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are there any objections from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no objections for the exhibits tendered by the Prosecution. I'm speaking on behalf of the Defence as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Masic. Ms. Hollis, do you have any objections as regards Exhibit D3/5?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. The exhibits will be tendered into evidence. Thank you very much, Ms. Hollis, for reminding me to tackle this issue. We are not going to start with another witness today for obvious reasons. We will see each other tomorrow again at 9.30, and as I have already indicated, tomorrow, in the afternoon at 4.00 we will have a Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 4th day of July, 2000 at 9.30 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
